about: A benchmark few residents have seen side by side: Harvard's schools, home of The Bromfield School, against Lunenburg's, on the state's one all-funds measure. The gap, how it has grown, where it goes, and the caveat that the two districts serve different populations. Links to the new Harvard and Bromfield pages.

text: Harvard's public schools, home of The Bromfield School, spend {hp.facts[id=gap].value.text} more on each student than Lunenburg's.

In {hp.finding.figures.y.text} Harvard spent {hp.facts[id=har].value.text} per student, counting every source of money. Lunenburg spent {hp.facts[id=lun].value.text}. The state median was {hp.facts[id=smed].value.text}. Ranked from the most spent per student to the least, Harvard placed {hp.facts[id=hrank].value.text} districts and Lunenburg {hp.facts[id=lrank].value.text}.

Where the difference goes: teachers are the biggest piece, {hl.facts[id=tgap].value.text} per student more. And grants and revolving funds, money outside the town's own appropriation, paid {hl.facts[id=gsh].value.text} of Harvard's spending, against {hl.facts[id=lgsh].value.text} of Lunenburg's.

The caveat that matters: the two districts serve different students. {hp.facts[id=li].value.text} of Harvard's students are low-income, against {hp.facts[id=li].label.figures.l.text} of Lunenburg's. Nothing here shows that spending more causes better results, or that spending less has changed them; comparing two districts cannot separate spending from everything else that differs.
If you could ask Harvard's school committee one question about how they spend, what would it be? Tell us in the comments.
